newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Fidelity faces its customers.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Fidelity faces its customers.

text.p: Fidelity Investments, whose officials are meeting with top clients in six cities this month, said Tuesday it hopes to address concerns about its performance and recent fund manager departures.

"The road trip was an effort to go out and meet with our customers," Paul Hondros, president of Fidelity's retail group, told Reuters. "We know there were concerns (among customers) about 1996 performance and management turnover."
"(Our customers) want assurance that our larger funds are being run the way they expect them to be run," he said.

"It's hit us all that there's a real appetite for hearing from us, not just on issues and concerns, but also on where we see the markets going, how our portfolio managers are positioning the portfolios," Hondros said.

Boston-based Fidelity, with total managed assets of $496.3 billion as of December 31, is the nation's largest provider 401(k) retirement services and the second-largest discount brokerage. It offers 249 mutual funds managed by more than 460 research, trading and portfolio management professionals.

Fidelity is facing audiences that are well aware that Vanguard Group's index funds took market share from Fidelity last year, and that four of Fidelity's fund managers have announced their departures since December, including managers in charge of portfolios worth a total of at least $16.6 billion.
A Fidelity spokeswoman said Tuesday that replacements for fixed-income managers Michael Gray and Bob Ives would be named within weeks.
The current Fidelity road show, scheduled to end January 30 in Boston, is also designed to collect feedback from customers other than institutional clients, Hondros said.

"This (meeting with smaller customers) is a new kind of way of doing things for Fidelity," Hondros said. "We're going to come back again in about six months and visit another six cities, probably come back here to Chicago."
Hondros said upcoming tours may not be on as large a scale as the current shows, which he said are drawing between 2,500 and 3,500 people in each of the cities visited so far.
Hondros said Fidelity would also spend less on its advertising campaigns in 1997 than last year.
"We don't publish (the figure), but we will spend less in 1997 that we did in 1996," Hondros said.
"We're also changing the composition of how we advertise," Hondros said. "We're going back to cable and print. We had gotten away from print (ads) in previous years.
Hondros said the company most recently focused its ad spending on major broadcast networks.
Fidelity now plans to give its campaigns more of an educational bent, Hondros said.
"The sophistication level of the customer is changing," he said. "They read more, they know more and they're smarter about their options.
